24V AC solenoid valves MOSFET

Other Hardware General Electronics
andrpex April 12, 2017, 6:22pm 1
Dear all, I'm planning to include the garden irrigation system on my DIY home automation system. The existing solenoid valves are 24V AC. I've a lot of IRFZ44N and a bunch of IRLZ44. Do you think that they can do the job? What resistor should I put between them and the Arduino Pro Mini digital pins? Thanks!
PieterP April 12, 2017, 6:43pm 2
You need a relay or a triac to switch AC. MOSFETs can only switch DC.
To drive a MOSFET, you need a small gate resistor (to limit the current when switching, since the gate is basically a capacitor) and a pull-down resistor to keep the gate voltage from drifting when nothing is connected. You also need a flyback diode when switching inductive loads like solenoids.
It's better to use an IRLZ44 over an IRFZ44N because it's a logic-level MOSFET. The 5V output from the Arduino is not high enough to drive the IRFZ44N.

The reality is that relay contacts switching AC power will spark. That is just how it works. And if the contacts are applied to operate within their design limits then it is OK for that to happen. Relays have a predicted life span number of operations at their rated load, and they are not generally claimed to last forever, although it sometimes seems that they do. So a bit of spark when relay contacts open is not a problem, except in locations where there are vapors present that may be ignited by that spark. Relays switching DC loads should be rated for the DC operation, which is often much less

In this post I am using DC voltage solenoid valves only. Valves that use AC have very different requirements and the below does not apply. Most DC solenoid valves tend to use a voltage any where from 6v up and 12V and 24V are very common. The one I am using below is 24v. The Arduino cannot handle these voltages and so cannot (or should not) be connected directly to the valve. Instead, we use another device as a middleman, one that can accept the 5v signal from the Arduino as a control signal and also handle the higher voltage and current required by the valve.

The TIP120 can handle 60v up to 5 amps. These are the maximum ratings so the TIP120 should not really be used at this level. My valve is 24V and rated for 0.275 amps so well within the

...

N-channel mosfets are voltage driven and require very little current. They also have very little voltage drop across drain-source. The actual voltage drop is dependent on the mosfets RDS(on) property. So the lower the RDS(on) the better. The IRLZ44N has a RDS(on) of 17.5mΩ, not bad, and can handle 55v at 49 amps (remember these are maximum ratings, don’t actually use it at this level).
I am using the mosfet as a switch exactly like the TIP120. But why bother with a

...

Flyback Diode

When you remove power from an electromagnet, the magnetic field collapses creating current (the coil is an inductive load). This current can be very high and can be powerful enough to kill an Arduino. To stop this happening we add a flyback diode (AKA a snubber diode, freewheeling diode, and many other names). The diode allows current to move in one direction only and safely dissipates the current created by the collapsing magnetic field. This can slow the decay slightly but for use with solenoids this is not noticeable, the valve is much slower.

uld not use one) a diode for AC solenoids. A diode will try and rectify the AC wave to a half wave. Bad idea.
Secondly, the spec sheet mentions that the module features:
groov 12–250 VAC output modules are used to switch up to 12 separate AC loads. They provide 300 volts of transient protection between field signals and the logic side of the modules. AC outputs are zero voltage turn on and zero current turn off to minimize transients during switching.
This means that they will turn on when the AC voltage is passing through zero volts your solenoid will get a ‘soft turn on’ as the voltage ramps up. On a turn off command, the module will only switch off when it sees the AC current flowing to the solenoid is at zero. If the current is zero when it turns off then there is no back lash so no RC (resistor capacitor) snubber circuit is needed.
Bottom line is to remove the diode and don’t worry about putting in a snubber circuit.
The one thing you DO need to worry about that you did not mention is the VA or wattage of each solenoid valve. The current rating of the module is 0.5 amps per channel. That’s straight resistive, but the solenoid might be more inductive so its spec sheet should be consulted to see what its max rating is.

Screenshot 2025-04-04 at 8.58.32 AM.png The reason you DON'T see a spark when using an AC source (not DC) is that the AC source voltage crosses zero 120 times every second. There's a chance you MIGHT see a spark but only if you happen to open the switch while the AC Sine Wave is at or near either peak. Opening the switch at the exact right moment will give you a spark, but not as strong a spark when using DC. That's because AC is typically measured at RMS value (Root Mean Square).

excerpts:
Even when the per-point rating is sufficient (2 A on a 23 mA solenoid, for example), the relay output on a PLC has a limited mechanical life and a limited electrical life under inductive load. PLC output relay manufacturers typically rate the contacts at 100,000 to 300,000 operations at full rated resistive load; switching an unsuppressed inductive load drops that figure by an order of magnitude. The field practice is to never switch the solenoid directly from the PLC output regardless of the published rating.

2. Contact rating exceeds the solenoid inrush current by at least 3x.

For DC coils (24 VDC proportional or 24 VDC on/off), a logic-level SSR with a MOSFET output is the modern preferred choice: no moving parts, no contact bounce, no inrush problem at the SSR output.

* RC snubber | Resistor + capacitor in series, across coil | AC coils (220/110 VAC) | R approx 10-100 kOhm, C approx 0.1-0.47 uF, 630 V rating
* MOV | Metal-oxide varistor across coil | AC coils, especially 220/240 VAC | Clamp voltage ~275-320 V (275 VAC MOV for 220 VAC coil)
* Flyback diode | 1N4007 or fast-recovery diode, cathode to +V | DC coils only | Slow turn-off; doubles release time
